Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

It records the names of members and regular collaborators who may enter outside staffed hours. The current sheet took effect on March 1, after the winter schedule ended. A blue mark beside a name means that person has an active door code; it does not indicate permission to use every room or piece of equipment. The list is reviewed at the start of each month, but changes can be requested at any time.

Mara Ellison manages the list and handles requests from members, visiting instructors, and project partners. She checks each request against the person’s membership or the message from the staff member hosting them. When someone is added, Mara records the date, the expected length of access, and the rooms they may use. A member who needs only the print room, for example, is not automatically given access to the recording booth. The paper copy is useful during a network outage, while the digital file makes it easier to track the history of changes.

1. Updating an entry

Requests to add or remove a name should be sent to Mara by email or left in the labeled tray at the front desk. Each request needs the person’s full name and the reason for the change. For a temporary collaborator, it should also include a final access date. A request from a project partner must identify the member responsible for hosting that person. Mara confirms the details before editing the list, and the host remains responsible for telling their guest which doors and areas are available to them.

After making a change, Mara writes the update date in the margin of the paper sheet and saves the digital file with the same date in its filename. She does not erase the previous version immediately. Older copies are kept in a folder for three months so that staff can check when a code was issued or removed if a question arises. The current paper sheet is then placed back in the cabinet, and the front desk is told that its copy has changed. Staff members are not expected to circulate the full list, since it contains personal contact details as well as access information.

The list is not a substitute for a room booking. People with general studio access still need to reserve the photography bay, the kiln room, or the large worktable when those spaces are scheduled for a class. A door code lets an authorized person enter the building; it does not hold equipment for them. The calendar at the front desk shows bookings, maintenance closures, and times when a room has been assigned to a workshop. If an entry on the access sheet seems to conflict with the calendar, the person should check with the staff member who made the booking rather than assume the room is available.

Mara described the distinction during a February staff meeting: “The list answers who can get in, and the calendar answers which space is in use.” The note was added to the meeting record because two visiting artists had arrived for a booked session and found the photography bay occupied by a class. Both artists had building access, but their reservation was for a different time. The studio manager moved the class to the worktable, and the artists began their session after the bay had been cleared. The incident did not lead to a change in the access list, but it prompted staff to check that booking confirmations name the room as well as the date.

Some entries have an end date, while others stay active until a member leaves or asks for a change. Visiting instructors usually receive access for the dates of their courses, including setup time when it has been arranged in advance. Project partners may need a longer period, especially when they are working on an installation that takes several weeks. Mara does not extend a temporary entry simply because the person has used the studio before. The host must send a new request if the original end date no longer fits the project schedule.

When a member reports that a code has been shared or used unexpectedly, Mara marks the entry for review and contacts the member before changing it. Staff do not assume that a report is accurate until they have checked the access record and heard from the people involved. If a code needs to be disabled while the review is underway, the studio manager can arrange that separately. The access sheet records whether the code is active, but it does not contain notes about a dispute or a staff conversation. Those details are kept in the manager’s incident file, which is stored apart from the list.

The front desk has a short checklist for checking the current copy. At opening, staff confirm that the cabinet is locked and that the date on the paper sheet matches the date in the digital filename. They also make sure the labeled request tray is empty or that any new notes have been passed to Mara. If a staff member notices a mismatch, they do not copy one version over the other; they tell Mara which dates they found and leave both files unchanged until she checks them. During a busy event, the desk may be covered by a substitute, so the checklist is kept beside the cabinet rather than in the staff scheduling folder.

At the end of April, Mara plans to review the entries for the spring ceramics residency. The residency has three visiting artists, one local technician, and a host member who will be in the studio most weekdays. Their access dates are different because one artist will arrive later than the others, and the technician is scheduled for two installation days only. Mara has the dates from the residency coordinator but is waiting for the host member to confirm which rooms will be used. Until that detail is settled, she has not added the visiting group to the current sheet.
